notes.meaning: Luke begins by noting that several other writers had already tried to write down the story of Jesus. These accounts described the events that had come to pass, fulfilling what God had promised in the Old Testament.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars view this opening as a typical Greco-Roman historical preface that blends historical facts with creative storytelling.

notes.meaning: The information about Jesus was passed down by the original eyewitnesses and those who preached the gospel. Luke was not an eyewitness himself, but he received the truth from the apostles and others who were with Jesus from the start.

Luke decided to write his own careful, well-arranged history after thoroughly checking every detail from the start. He addressed the book to Theophilus, a respected man who likely helped pay for the project or needed a clear record.

Luke wrote so that Theophilus would have complete confidence in the teachings he had already received. Hearing the gospel is good, but having a trustworthy written record helps settle any doubts and gives firm grounding.

The story moves to the historical reign of Herod the Great in Judea. A Jewish priest named Zechariah served in the priestly group of Abijah, and his wife Elizabeth was also from the family line of Aaron.

Both Zechariah and Elizabeth were devoted followers of God who lived pure and obedient lives. Being called blameless did not mean they were sinless, but that they faithfully followed God's laws and commands with an honest heart.

The couple had no children because Elizabeth was unable to have a baby, and both had grown old. In that culture, childlessness brought great social sorrow and shame, yet God was preparing to show His supernatural power.
Zechariah's division took its regular turn to serve God in the temple for a week. Priests carried out their sacred tasks before the Lord with reverence and careful attention to God's law.

Priests drew lots to decide who received each special temple duty, and the lot chose Zechariah to burn incense in the sanctuary. Because there were thousands of priests, this high honour was a rare privilege that usually came only once in a lifetime.

Outside the inner building, a large crowd of worshippers gathered to pray while the incense was being offered. The smoke of the incense going up to heaven was a picture of the people's prayers rising to God.

While Zechariah was inside, an angel of the Lord suddenly appeared on the right side of the incense altar. Seeing a heavenly messenger was a powerful sign that God was breaking hundreds of years of silence.
When Zechariah saw the angel, he was deeply startled and overcome with terror. Coming face to face with God's heavenly glory often brings deep fear and awe to mortal human beings.

The angel told Zechariah not to be afraid because God had heard his prayer. He announced that Elizabeth would give birth to a son, and that they must name the boy John, which means God has shown favor.

This child would bring immense joy and gladness to his parents, and many others would celebrate his birth. People would rejoice because this baby was chosen to bring the good news of God's coming salvation.

John would be great in the Lord's eyes and would live a life set apart for God, never drinking wine or strong drink. Instead of being influenced by alcohol, he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even before he was born.

differ.view: Anglicans point to this verse to show that infants are capable of receiving God's grace and the Holy Spirit, supporting the practice of baptizing babies into the church.
Baptists understand the Spirit's filling here as God's special prophetic calling on an unborn person rather than an argument for infant baptism.

notes.meaning: John's ministry would lead many people in Israel to turn away from their sins and return to the Lord their God. His preaching would awaken hearts and call God's wandering people to true repentance.

John would go ahead of the Lord with the same boldness, power, and courage that the ancient prophet Elijah had. He would heal family relationships and guide disobedient people back to godly wisdom, getting them ready to welcome the Lord.

Zechariah questioned the angel, asking how he could be sure of this promise since he and his wife were very old. Instead of trusting God's word, he looked at his physical limitations and asked for proof.
The angel identified himself as Gabriel, who stands in the direct presence of God and carries His messages. He told Zechariah that he was sent directly by God to bring this joyful news of salvation.

Because Zechariah did not believe the angel's message, he was struck mute until the promise came true. This loss of speech served as both a discipline for his doubt and a sign that God's word would surely happen.

Outside the temple building, the crowd waited for Zechariah to come out and give them the traditional priestly blessing. They began to wonder why he was taking so much longer than usual in the holy place.

When Zechariah finally stepped outside, he was completely unable to speak to the waiting crowd. By his silent gestures and motions, the people realized he had seen a supernatural vision in the sanctuary.
Even though Zechariah could not speak, he stayed at the temple and faithfully finished his full week of priestly duties. Once his assigned days of service were done, he returned to his home.
Shortly after Zechariah returned home, Elizabeth became pregnant just as the angel had foretold. She chose to stay in quiet seclusion for five months, taking time to reflect and give thanks to God.
Elizabeth praised the Lord for His kindness in giving her a child in her old age. In Israelite society, being unable to bear children was seen as a public disgrace, but God took away her shame.

In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, God sent the angel Gabriel on another mission, this time to the region of Galilee. He went to Nazareth, a small and quiet village far away from the religious center of Jerusalem.

Gabriel was sent to a young virgin named Mary, who was legally pledged to marry a man named Joseph from the royal line of King David. In Jewish culture, this betrothal was a binding agreement that came before the wedding and living together.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition reads Mary's virginity and betrothal alongside her later question in verse 34 as evidence that she had taken a vow of lifelong virginity.
